prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state as a Z2 topological phase protected by time-reversal symmetry, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B002 to B013, a single part to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The reason is scientific and not a head count. My own case for optical lattices rested on a discovery about emergent many-body matter, but when I try to write the citation and the three names I cannot do it cleanly: Bloch, Greiner and Zoller leave out Esslinger, Cirac and Jaksch, each with a defensible claim, and the committee would have to explain that choice. B013 does not have this problem. A theoretical prediction, that spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry give a Z2 invariant and protected edge channels, was tested in a clean experiment in which the HgTe wells showed the quantised edge conductance and its dependence on gate voltage and sample width. That conductance could have come out wrong and did not. Transport and photoemission experiments in several laboratories and material families have confirmed it for about eighteen years. For me that is the standard of robust agreement between theory and experiment, and B013 meets it better than my earlier choice. It also answers the question I care about, which is how a protected quantum state can survive in a real, disordered solid. I would keep the citation to the 2D quantum spin Hall state and its first observation, and not claim the whole class of topological insulators for these three people.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I do not want to hide it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal told Molenkamp which material and which thickness to try, and it lies outside the three names, with Zhang deceased. Hasan's ARPES work on three-dimensional topological insulators is an independent discovery and a trio built on the 2D story leaves it out. The 2016 prize also makes some members ask whether this is a second helping of topology. I still think B002 is the more novel question, and I may be biased towards atomic physics. B002 is now my first alternative, with its attribution unresolved. I am not a condensed matter specialist and rely on Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson for the finer points of who did what first in HgTe and in the 3D materials.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps Kane, Mele and Molenkamp but words the citation to end on establishing topological insulators as a new class of quantum matter, and he asks that the text explain why this differs from the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree that the citation must say why this is distinct, but I would not use his closing phrase. A class of matter that includes the 3D materials is exactly where Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang work sit, and three names cannot honestly carry it. My preference is the narrower wording: the quantum spin Hall state as a time-reversal-protected Z2 phase, and its first observation. It is a smaller claim and an accurate one, and its limits are visible in the text, which should make it easier to defend later. I accept his point that Kane and Mele cannot be separated, since the Z2 classification is a joint result.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B013 first on the closure of theory, first-principles band structure and measured spectra, and in round 1 proposed Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, which Danielsson reports he may swap for Mele.
responses.response: His closure argument is what moved me, and I now stand with it. On the swap I still disagree. Hasan's ARPES work is an excellent and original experimental discovery, but it belongs to the 3D branch, whereas the trio built on 2D has one prediction and one first observation of the same effect. Replacing Mele would leave the 2D prediction with only half its authors, and then Molenkamp's measurement would have no clearly credited theorist ahead of it. If the committee wants the 3D branch recognised, I think that is a separate achievement for a later year, and not a reason to alter this trio. I would like to hear from him whether he accepts the narrower scope.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a simple general Z2 classification, and that a single-achievement prize should not be diluted.
responses.response: I agree on keeping a single part, and I withdraw my round-1 suggestion that the 2016 prize lowers the novelty of B013. As I understand his point, the 2016 prize rewarded topological phase transitions and Hall-type phases whose invariants come from a magnetic field or from interactions, while here the invariant comes from spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry in a band structure with no applied field, and it gives edge channels which a transport experiment can observe. That is a one-sentence answer to the chair's question. I defer to him if he thinks it is imprecise in condensed matter terms.

responses.point: Kroll alone prefers optical lattice clocks (B006), arguing that the clocks are reproduced at 10^-18 and that I apply the discovery-versus-technique line unevenly against B006 while valuing B022.
responses.response: His criticism is fair and I accept it. Both B006 and B022 are measurement-first, and I have no good reason to rank one above the other on that ground, so I have stopped treating the discovery question as the main reason against B006. My remaining concerns are narrower: the redefinition of the second is pending, and priority around 2003 to 2005 and the ion-clock lineage is not settled in the material we have. I would not oppose a later prize on B006 to Katori and Ye, whose attribution he rightly says is clean. For this year I see B013 as the stronger and more complete story, and I note he places it first among his alternatives and ranked it low because it is outside his field.

responses.point: The chair asks whether Kroll and I would accept B013 alone and what second part or alternative we would put forward, and whether the citation can be accurate about people it omits.
responses.response: I would now accept B013 alone, and I do not want a second part, because adding B002 would bring back a five-name allocation for two seats and gain nothing scientifically. On the omissions, I think the citation can be accurate if it says exactly what these three did: Kane and Mele predicted the quantum spin Hall state and its Z2 classification, and Molenkamp observed it. The role of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of Hasan then belongs in the committee's background text, where it can be described openly, and not in the citation wording. For B002 my answer is that three of Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger and Cirac is not a split I can currently justify, which is part of why I moved.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the narrow 2D citation without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, or judges that a prize for the quantum spin Hall effect needs to name that step.
Whether my one-sentence distinction from the 2016 prize is accurate in condensed matter terms, which I cannot check without help from Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson.
Whether B013 is chosen too fast because it reflects the openings of other members, as the chair observes, and whether my own move partly reflects that.
For B002, the three-person split and the absence of Jaksch from the credited names, which I still cannot settle and which is why it stays an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups. None of the credited people for B013, B002 or B022 are among the collaborators named in my profile, so I report no specific conflict and I do not ask to recuse from B013.
